summary: Deep technical profiling call focused on GPU runtime behavior across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM backends. Covered kernel selection heuristics, CUDA graphs benefits/limitations, KV cache interactions with batching and quantization, and on-prem/VPC constraints. topics: KV cache behavior with batching and quantization
meeting_header: Date: 2026-04-10 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 55 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (CTO, Aperture), Devon Park (ML Eng), Lina Ko (Infra Lead)
transcript: 00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a minute, we want to run through the profiling we did and walk through kernel selection and cudagraphs 00:18 Ethan Rodriguez: hi - Ethan here, i'm the SE on runtime perf, i'll drive the profiling bits, we have a few artifacts i'll share after - some per-kernel traces, cuda graph snapshots, and a short dashboard 00:35 Sofia Alvarez: great thanks, we mainly want to understand the throughput/latency delta between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM for our L2R model, and implications for KV cache when we enable quantization 00:50 Devon Park: and secondarily the deployment constraints for our VPC setup, we have 8xA100s behind a private subnet and strict egress rules, so anything that requires outbound telemetry is tough 01:10 Ethan Rodriguez: understood. quick overview: our profiling ran on two backends: TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) with int8 calibration paths and vLLM with optimized kernels. we captured per-kernel timings via Nsight and traced cudagraph launches. results vary by sequence length distribution and batch shape 01:35 Lina Ko: can you clarify what you mean by "per-kernel"? like attention, gelu, matmul? 01:42 Ethan Rodriguez: yeah exactly - we break down matmuls (GEMM), attention kernels (QKV fusion where present), position-wise feedforward (GELU/FC), softmax, and KV cache memcpy/concat ops. TRT-LLM tends to fuse more ops which reduces kernel launch overhead but sometimes increases memory pressure 02:05 Maya Chen: high level tradeoff: TRT-LLM gives stronger single-request latency when you can fuse kernels and exploit tensor cores, vLLM gives better multi-request throughput with smaller overhead for dynamic batching and KV cache reuse 02:25 Devon Park: curious about cudagraphs — we've seen in-house that cudagraphs improve p99 but break with dynamic shapes, what's your experience? 02:35 Ethan Rodriguez: good point — cudagraphs are excellent when your execution graph is stable. we saw ~15-30% token throughput uplift on long, consistent sequences because they avoid repeated kernel launch overhead. but warmup and shape-change is a problem: if sequence length or batch size changes you need to re-capture graphs which can spike latency 03:00 Sofia Alvarez: does re-capture add a lot of overhead? like, if we re-capture every time traffic changes, that's not acceptable 03:08 Ethan Rodriguez: re-capture cost depends on model and graph complexity. for a 30B-style model capture can be hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds. Redwood's runtime attempts to amortize this by caching graphs keyed by shape signatures and falling back gracefully — but high variability in live traffic can reduce benefits 03:40 Devon Park: how does KV cache interact with batching and quant? we saw some degradation when enabling 4-bit quantization 03:50 Ethan Rodriguez: KV cache is sensitive: quantization reduces memory but some quant kernels need dequant/rehydrate steps for attention matmuls, which adds overhead. with 4-bit we saw ~5-12% latency increase on QKV path in some cases, but overall token cost reduced due to smaller memory bandwidth and higher batch packing 04:15 Maya Chen: and there's also the tradeoff of more cache misses if you shard KV across devices or store compressed KV, which can increase cross-device comms 04:30 Lina Ko: we are on a VPC with NCCL over private ethernet, cross-device cost is nontrivial for our topology 04:38 Ethan Rodriguez: important note — TRT-LLM's fused kernels sometimes reduce the need to shuttle intermediate activations, which helps for sharded KV setups. vLLM's design focuses on dynamic batching and efficient cache reuse; so depending on your shape distro you might prefer one 05:05 Sofia Alvarez: did you run any end-to-end numbers we can look at? p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec 05:12 Ethan Rodriguez: yes, quick snapshot: for Aperture's baseline config with seq len mostly 128-256 and batch 1-4: TRT-LLM (int8 tuned) -> p50 ~ 45ms/token, p95 ~ 78ms/token, tokens/sec ~ 2600. vLLM (fp16 optimized) -> p50 ~ 55ms/token, p95 ~ 92ms/token, tokens/sec ~ 3000 because of better batching. these are noisy; we'll share raw traces 05:45 Devon Park: interesting that vLLM had higher throughput; is that because of better batching? 05:50 Ethan Rodriguez: yep, vLLM incurs less graph rework for varied shapes and its batching logic keeps GPU occupancy higher for mixed small requests. TRT-LLM with cudagraphs beat vLLM on stable long sequences once captured 06:10 Maya Chen: we also looked at kernel-level breakdown — TRT-LLM reduces number of small GEMMs by fusing, so kernel launch time reduces by ~20-40% in some windows 06:28 Sofia Alvarez: any caveats on cudagraphs with NCCL or multi-GPU? we run model parallel + pipeline on some shards 06:36 Ethan Rodriguez: cudagraphs plus NCCL is tricky — collective comms inside graphs are supported but must be deterministic. we saw cases where NCCL collectives caused graph capture to be nonreplayable if timing varied. recommended pattern: capture with representative traffic and keep graceful fallback to non-graph path for spikes 07:05 Devon Park: about quantization: you mentioned int8 calibration for TRT-LLM and 4-bit for vLLM — which gave us better cost/perf? 07:14 Ethan Rodriguez: int8 TRT-LLM gave best latency for single requests with careful calibration but required a calibration dataset and validation. 4-bit in vLLM reduced memory footprint more and improved tokens/sec in heavy batching, but added some attention path overhead. pick based on your SLO: low-latency p95 -> TRT-LLM+int8, high throughput cost-efficient -> vLLM+4bit 07:45 Lina Ko: are there known stability bugs we should watch for in on-prem setups? driver versions, cuda/cuDNN combos etc 07:52 Ethan Rodriguez: yes - always pin CUDA/cuDNN and TRT versions. we saw divergence on CUDA 12.2 vs 12.1 for certain fused kernels, and some cuDNN autotune heuristics cause non-deterministic perf. Redwood maintains a compatibility matrix and we'll share it 08:10 Maya Chen: question from our side: how do you suggest we benchmark with our traffic? what's the minimal representative workload? 08:18 Ethan Rodriguez: ask for a 1-hour baseline with: request rate matching peak RPCs, sequence length distribution, distribution of batch arrival patterns (spiky vs uniform), and a small set of typical prompts. include cold-starts and reconfiguration events so we exercise cudagraph recapture 08:40 Devon Park: we can provide traffic trace and a bucketed seq len distribution, we'll attach that in the slack thread 08:48 Sofia Alvarez: what about observability and tracing hooks? we need per-token cost attribution and kernel-level flame graphs 08:55 Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports per-token latency/cost breakdown, and we can attach Nsight backtraces. Ethan will provide the per-kernel CSVs which you can import into your perf tools 09:10 Ethan Rodriguez: also watch out for memory fragmentation on long-running pods with quantize/dequant ops — we instrumented allocator metrics and found fragmentation increased over days for certain configs 09:28 Lina Ko: that'd be a blocker for long-running private clusters, we prefer predictable memory with recycled pods 09:35 Ethan Rodriguez: runsafe approach: periodic pod replacement or aggressive allocator tuning; also consider pinned memory arenas 09:45 Sofia Alvarez: any security notes re: cudagraph capture? seems benign but want to confirm no outbound telemetry 09:52 Maya Chen: no outbound telemetry required for capture; artifacts are local traces and graphs. Redwood's Private deployment keeps these inside the VPC and integrates with your KMS for keys if you want encrypted artifacts at rest 10:10 Devon Park: okay last technical: how does the runtime pick kernels at inference time? is it heuristic or measured? 10:18 Ethan Rodriguez: hybrid — compile-time heuristics plus runtime profile sampling. runtime will run a short microbenchmark for a new model shape and pick kernels (cuBLAS vs custom fused) and cache the selection. we also fall back based on memory headroom 10:40 Sofia Alvarez: great, that helps. any known incompatibilities with our enterprise compliance needs? we have SOC2 and required audit logs 10:48 Maya Chen: Redwood Private includes audit logs, RBAC, SSO/SAML support and we can provide SOC2 documentation — Maya will include links 11:05 Ethan Rodriguez: ok the artifacts we'll send: per-kernel CSVs, cudagraph snapshots, a short runbook for capture and recommended driver matrix 11:20 Maya Chen: recap and next steps: Ethan to share kernel-level profiling tarball, Maya will send security & pricing docs, Aperture to share traffic shape and schedule baseline run. book follow-up for week of 2026-04-20 11:40 Sofia Alvarez: sound good, thanks everyone 11:45 Devon Park: thanks, appreciate the detail, we'll get the traces over by monday 11:50 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in slack and email with links
